1.1 Main risk channels

The vulnerability of the financial system at large is derived from the vulnerability of its main risk channels. In the
Report for the first half of 2023, five main channels were analyzed:
Macroeconomic environment—the domestic and global macroeconomic environment affects economic activity
and resilience of the main players in the financial system—households, companies, and financial intermediaries.
The more solid and the more stable the macroeconomic environment is and the more positive the outlooks for its
development are, the less vulnerable is the system.
Asset prices—the financial system becomes more vulnerable if asset prices in its operating environment deviate
from the fundamentals or from their long-term trend and if its prices change due to underpricing of risks. In such

from the fundamentals or from their long-term trend and if its prices change due to underpricing of risks. In such
an environment, there is heightened risk of an abrupt correction in the prices of financial and/or real assets that
may cascade into an adverse impact on the financial system.
Credit—when households and businesses take large amounts of credit (leveraging), they expose themselves to
risks that stem inter alia from an upturn in interest rates (insofar as they borrow at variable rates), a downturn
in domestic or global economic activity, and a decrease in asset prices. The levels, distribution, and rapidity of
change in leveraging and in the uses of credit impact the vulnerability of the financial system.

change in leveraging and in the uses of credit impact the vulnerability of the financial system.
Liquidity—liquidity is a channel through which shocks may evolve into a financial crisis. The more liquid a market
is, the more assets can change hands while less value is lost. The levels of liquidity of banks and the business
sector determine their ability to cope, in the short term, with shocks to cash flow and economic activity.
Interconnectedness—the level of interconnectedness within the financial system, i.e., the strength of direct and
indirect exposures (via shared exposures to a third party, be it a real or a financial services company) among
banking institutions, institutional investors, and nonbanking entities determine how quickly shocks ripple

banking institutions, institutional investors, and nonbanking entities determine how quickly shocks ripple
through the system at large. Strong interconnectedness makes the financial system more vulnerable.

In addition to the environment in which the financial system operates and with the risk channels and the intensity
of their vulnerability treated as given, current risk scenarios determine the level of financial stability. In crisis-free
times—those typified by low volatility and absence of extreme events—the risk scenarios and the assessment
of the likelihood of their actualization are based on subjective judgment and influenced by many background
factors. To produce these scenarios, the Bank of Israel monitors global and domestic developments and consults
surveys by international and domestic institutions, investment houses, and rating companies in order to obtain
a broad perspective and different views. It also tracks the public discourse and trends in various global and

1.3 Resilience of the financial system

As the analytical framework (Figure 1) shows, the stability of the financial system ultimately depends on the
resilience of its components—their ability to absorb shocks that beset it along main channels of exposure. The
system’s resilience is assessed on the basis of stress tests and simulations—accounting tests predicated on the
balance sheets of the financial institutions and the activity segments—and focus on testing the solvency of the
banks and insurance companies and the resilience of the financial infrastructures, namely, the domestic payment
and settlement systems.4

   was abetted by the resilience and stability of the banking system and the insurance companies and the
   sound functioning of financial infrastructures (payment and settlement systems). The safety cushions
    that households and firms had built up—for reasons including the fiscal incentives and monetary easing
    that occurred during the COVID-19 period—made them more resilient to potential shocks.
•   During the period reviewed, the domestic financial system was affected by two main factors: 1)
   continued monetary tightening and slowing of economic growth in Israel and abroad, coupled with

    in the medium term.

market conditions, reflecting an upturn in system vulnerability along all risk channels—particularly in real-estate
credit, in which historically high-risk indicators persisted. The safety cushions that households and firms had
built up—due to the fiscal incentives and monetary loosening during the COVID-19 period, inter alia6—improved

The recent upturns in interest and inflation rates triggered an acute increase in the monthly payback of holders
of housing loans.40 This, however, may only partly reflect the change in households’ total debt burden at that

the monthly payback on existing nonhousing loans, creating liquidity difficulties that may incentivize some
households to take new loans and/or restructure existing ones. Alternatively, some households may choose to
use savings to pay back some of their outstanding debt in order to reduce their exposure to interest rate hikes and
inflation upturns.

Interconnectedness remained a low risk channel in the period reviewed. This assessment originates
in relatively low direct exposure among main players in the financial system and from relatively low, in
historical terms, indirect exposure in the banking system via credit to joint borrowers. The institutional
entities’ portfolios of domestic assets, however, remain highly similar. A potential of transfer of shocks
from regulated credit companies to the rest of the financial system exists as well.

Given that Israel has no significant interbank loan market, direct exposure is not a channel that can transmit a
shock from one bank to another bank or to the entire banking system. Shocks may, however, pass through on
another channel, an indirect one: shared exposure to the same borrowers.65 Although there is no criterion with
which to determine when a given level of exposure is too high, one may see from historical perspective that the
banks’ exposure to shared borrowers has been trending down and was not high at the most recent point in time

In this section, we examine risk scenarios to the Israeli financial system, including shocks transmitted and amplified
by main exposure channels and that, for this reason, exacerbate the vulnerability of the financial system and the
economy at large. In view of developments in the half-year reviewed, including the actualization of several risk
scenarios, we focus on their protracted foreseen impact, including the inertia factor. In our estimation, three main
risks evolved in the first half of the year: (1) slowing of activity, sticky inflation, and continued monetary tightening;
(2) a downturn in economic sentiment and performance in the wake of the legislative process; and (3) geopolitical

(2) a downturn in economic sentiment and performance in the wake of the legislative process; and (3) geopolitical
risks. Some of these risks operate along the same channels of transmission; therefore, their foreseen effects are
not independent of each other. Since the general equilibrium (the cumulative aggregate effect) is hard to estimate,
each risk must be discussed in itself, meaning that some simplification must take place.

1.      Activity slowdown, sticky inflation, and continued monetary tightening risk

The fact that Israel is a small and open economy that trades extensively and has a financial system heavily dependent
on international financial markets carries potential implications for financial stability and the transmission of
risks to domestic activity. Beyond the risks originating in the continued domestic monetary tightening, which
may exacerbate vulnerabilities along the credit channel (cost of credit servicing and credit allocation) and the
assets channel (particularly via the housing market),67 an additional effect on Israel in this scenario will take place
along the macro and financial-markets channel.

6. Resilience of the financial system

Given that some of the shocks already came to pass during the review period, the stability of the financial
system depends heavily today (much as it did during the COVID-19 pandemic) on the resilience of the financial
institutions, their infrastructures, and their ability to provide the safety margins that are needed for the continued
proper functioning of the system.

6.3 Payment and settlement systems

a. General remarks

a. General remarks

The controlled payment systems—Zahav (real-time gross settlement system), Masav (credit, debit and transfer
of payments system), the Automated Teller Machine system, and the payment card transaction system—show
high-level operating capabilities. These abilities are reflected in high scores on indices that include the percent
of operational availability and processing of transactions relative to maximum system capacity at a given time.
Alongside their strong operating resilience, most of the controlled payment systems are typified by moderate-
to-high concentration due to the small number of highly active participants in each system. These participants,
however, do not operate in a way that makes them dependent on each other in respect of liquidity.

2020. These products make a negative contribution to the solvency ratio because their capital requirement is larger than their contribution to economic
capital. Therefore, the emptying of this portfolio over time makes a substantive positive contribution to the solvency ratio.

b. Controlled payment systems

A payment system is a set of rules, instruments, or procedures for the dispatch and performance of payment
instructions among its participants; it comprises the participants and the system operator. Payment systems may
be composed of rules and procedures only or may also have a physical infrastructure. Payment orders are sent to
and from the financial entities that belong to the system (hereinafter: “participants in payment systems”101) and
are carried out atop technical infrastructures that are called FMIs.102
The financial entities that participate in the FMIs settle financial liabilities that they create among each other
pursuant to various daily operations in the domestic economy—payment card transactions, credit and debit

pursuant to various daily operations in the domestic economy—payment card transactions, credit and debit
transactions, checks, operations on the stock exchange, foreign-currency exchange, ATM transactions, etc.
Final reckonings among financial entities that keep local-currency accounts with the central bank are concluded
in the real-time system (Zahav). The Zahav system plays two main roles: final clearing of bilateral payment orders
that its participants initiate in the course of the business day, and final multilateral clearing of financial liabilities
that were previously processed in other domestic payment systems.103 These systems include the Masav system,
in which credit, debit and payment transfer transactions, including immediate ones, are made; Automated Teller

in which credit, debit and payment transfer transactions, including immediate ones, are made; Automated Teller
Machine system that links the ATMs of Israel’s banking system, payment card transaction system, a system of
payment card services; a securities clearing house, the MAOF clearing house; a check-based clearing house, and
the CLS system for foreign currency exchange.104
When payment systems malfunction, they may cause major havoc in the country’s financial system and may
even result in contagion to other participants in the systems, particularly at times of financial crisis. In an extreme
scenario, a participant in the system who defaults may trigger the default of additional participants. For example,

scenario, a participant in the system who defaults may trigger the default of additional participants. For example,
when participants are strongly dependent on liquidity flows from a participant who has defaulted, they may have
to use liquid sources outside the system until a situation in which they may reach insolvency.
We examined the stability of Israel’s controlled payment systems via three indicators: transaction processing
capacity, availability, and concentration.105

Transaction capacity

If a payment system experiences a failure event, the amount of time that passes from the detection and treatment
of the event to the full restoration of system activity is important. The more time lapses between the failure
event and its end, the more operating pressures, such as a backlog of payment orders awaiting processing, can
accumulate. These operating pressures may have an adverse effect on the system and its components, impair
participants’ liquidity management, harm the reputation of the service that the system provides its participants,
and so on.

Availability

The mere number of transactions processed yields no information about the systems’ operational performance.
For participants to be able to use the system’s services uninterruptedly and safely, payment systems need to
offer their participants different levels of availability. The payment-system operators calculate the availability
parameter as the ratio of the time a payment system operates in a given year to the maximum time that the system
should have operated that year. According to the international principles of financial-market infrastructures—the
PFMI—in the case of a failure event, payment systems should resume their operations rapidly, within two hours of
the eruption of the event at the latest.

Concentration

When one participant (or multiple participants) in a payment system accounts for an especially large share

concentration may point to a pattern of activity typified by dependency of the other participants on those who
generate a large share of activity.107 Figure 6.6 presents the level of concentration in Israel’s controlled payment
systems by means of the Herfindahl-Hirschman index.

1. General Assessment
In order to assess the risk to the stability of the financial system, the level of vulnerability in the

risk channels and the level of risk in potential scenarios were evaluated relative to the resilience

and absorptive capacity of the financial institutions. In the first half of 2024, despite the impact

on macroeconomic channels and on asset prices and the geopolitical scenario of escalating

tensions, financial institutions demonstrated strong resilience, including adequate capital ratios,

liquidity, and buffers. A low government debt-to-GDP ratio at the onset of the war and high

liquidity, and buffers. A low government debt-to-GDP ratio at the onset of the war and high

foreign exchange reserves held by the Bank of Israel have also contributed to the financial

system's stability.

  During this period, the macroeconomic risk level remained high, as in the previous report,

although there are signs of economic recovery compared to the early stages of the Swords of

Iron War, such as improvement in private consumption, exports, and the labor market.

Nonetheless, the government deficit has deepened and government bond yields have risen, both

in shekel terms and in terms of foreign currency, and the cost of financing government

expenditures has increased accordingly.4 The credit rating agencies have downgraded Israel's

expenditures has increased accordingly.4 The credit rating agencies have downgraded Israel's

credit rating and outlook due to heightened uncertainty regarding the potential expansion of the

war to additional fronts, the timeline for ending the fighting in Gaza, and the increased

fiscal/defense needs.

report. Domestic stock indices increased during the reviewed period, but at a relatively low rate.

Valuations relative to corporate profitability and major global stock indices continued to decline

to particularly low levels. The poor performance of the local stock exchange, which persisted

2. Risk Exposure Channels
The vulnerability of the financial system as a whole is derived from the level of exposure of its

main risk channels. The report for the first half of 2024 analyzes three primary risk channels:

      The macroeconomic channel (economic activity): The local macroeconomic environment

        affects economic activity and the resilience of key players in the financial system—

       households, companies, and financial intermediaries. The less stable this environment

households, companies, and financial intermediaries. The less stable this environment

      and the more volatile or negative the forecasts of its trend, the higher will be the system's

        vulnerability.

       Asset price channel: The financial system's vulnerability will increase  if asset prices

       deviate significantly from their fundamentals or their long-term trends, particularly due

       to underpricing of risk. In such an environment, there is an elevated risk of sharp

       corrections in financial and/or real asset prices, potentially affecting the financial system.

       Credit channel: High levels of credit provided to households and businesses (i.e., leverage)

   Credit channel: High levels of credit provided to households and businesses (i.e., leverage)

      expose them to various risks, such as interest rate increases (especially in the case of

       variable-rate credit), declines in local or global economic activity, and falling asset prices.

      The level of leverage, its distribution and its rate of change, and the uses of credit all

       influence the financial system's vulnerability.

   5.3. The effect of ETFs on the yields and liquidity of the base assets

Main findings

   In recent years, the passive investment fund market in Israel has experienced steady growth,
    as was also observed in global trends.

  This box focuses on cases of shares being added to the TA-125 Index and examines the
    contribution of exchange-traded funds (ETFs) to their price movements and trading volumes
   on the stock exchange as a result of index updates.

   It was found that the average trading volume of shares that are about to be included in the TA-
   125 Index increases sharply the day before, though there is a trend of rising trading volumes
    several weeks before.

  The increase in trading volume is accompanied by higher returns for stocks that are expected
    to be added to the index; however, their prices begin to decline after the event.

  The significant spike in trading volume around the entry day results from the inelastic demand
   by passive investment funds, which is the result of the regulatory requirement that they adjust
    their exposure to the new stock.

   In addition, public information about the date of an index update and the publicly known
    criteria for a stock’s inclusion allow noninstitutional and often non-Israeli investors to exploit
    this situation for profit.

    1. Background

1. Background

  For over a decade, the global ETF market has experienced steady growth. As of the end of the
first quarter of 2024, ETFs worldwide managed assets totaling approximately $11.38 trillion, most
of which (around $9.2 trillion) is invested in equities. In the US, ETFs hold about 12.7 percent of
all equities in the market, valued at approximately $6.5 trillion, while in Europe, they hold about
8.5 percent, with a total value of approximately $1.2 trillion.

  With the rise in the popularity of ETFs, there has been growing interest in their potential effects
on the assets they own. In general, it has been found that ETFs contribute positively to the liquidity





                                         57

57

of their underlying assets.47 This effect is evident when comparing to the period before the
inclusion of the asset or to similar unincluded stocks. Moreover, ETFs provide diversification to
investors in a simple way and with low management fees.

However, ETFs may also pose risks to financial stability. For example, during market crises,
particularly in the case of flash crashes,48 American ETFs have faced significant liquidity
challenges. This phenomenon ultimately led the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC)
to introduce a regulation in 2010 which, under certain conditions, required the suspension of ETF
trading during flash crashes. This regulation was first applied in August 2015,49 resulting in the
suspension of trading for over 300 ETFs until the crisis passed. From a macroeconomic perspective
of financial stability, studies have found that ETFs tend to increase the comovement (correlation)
in the returns of underlying assets, which may amplify market volatility.50

It was  also found  that  attempts by
sophisticated investors to exploit ETFs
for  arbitrage  profits may  affect  the
underlying assets in a number of ways.
First, ETFs  can  increase  the  price
volatility  of  the  underlying  assets
relative to other assets. This is due to
investors' attempts to obtain arbitrage
profits   from   price   discrepancies
between the ETF and the prices of the underlying assets, as well as the transmission of shocks
from ETFs to their underlying assets.51 Studies have also found that investors, and in particular
hedge funds, may exploit the transparency of ETFs and the regulatory need to rebalance the ETF's
asset composition at predetermined times. This can lead to high trading costs for ETFs and

  The most common means  of passive

As also observed in global trends, in recent years there has been a growing trend in Israel toward

    2. Methodology and findings

As of today, the TA-125 Index is updated twice a year, in May and November, with an official
public announcement about the new stocks to be included in the index made approximately two
weeks prior to their inclusion. However, the public is aware of the criteria for a stock's inclusion
in the index, allowing analysts to predict which stocks are likely to enter the index even before the
official announcement.

The analysis focuses on the inclusion
of new stocks  in  the TA-125  Index.
Between 2021 and 2024, there were 39
stocks added to the index, of which 35
were  already  traded  on  the  stock
exchange prior to their inclusion. The
analysis compares two groups of stocks:
the treatment group, consisting of stocks
that entered the index (the “125th stock"),
and the control group, consisting of stocks that did not enter the index but were closest in market
value to the "125th stock" on the day of inclusion.55 The day a stock enters the index is defined as
"Day 0," and various developments before and after are examined using a window of 150 days
before and 100 days after Day 0. Of the new stocks included in the index during the described

before and 100 days after Day 0. Of the new stocks included in the index during the described
period, 18 were traded throughout all the relevant time windows, and these were used for
comparison purposes. We examine the trading volumes of the stocks and their cumulative returns.
The data we rely on is "Smart Money" data from the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange.

55 There are only a few cases in which multiple stocks entered the index on the same day. In such instances, the weight
of the next stock in line that did not enter the index was doubled in the control group, in order to maintain numerical
balance between the treatment group and the control group.

If the dynamics described above are directly related to the extent of passive investment in ETFs
and index adjustments, we would expect to see the opposite trend when a stock is removed from
the index. Indeed, an analysis using the same methodology of approximately 40 stocks removed
from the index confirmed this inverse relationship: trading volumes spike sharply near the event,
ETFs become the largest net sellers, and foreign investors (in this case, also private Israeli
investors) are the largest net buyers. The selling occurs while the exiting stock's price is declining.

The findings described here reflect movements in trading volume and stock returns that are
connected to passive investment in the stock market and the method of updating stock indices on
the exchange. While the entry (and conversely, the exit) of a stock makes it more attractive to
many market players, it also creates rigid demand due to the regulatory requirement of passive
investment funds that are focused on a specific index to adjust their exposure to the new stock

Moreover, the behavior of various market players near the time of a stock’s inclusion indicates
that public information regarding the update schedules for the index and criteria for inclusion likely
enable certain investors—often non-institutional and typically non-Israeli investors—to exploit
this situation for profit. These investors anticipate a future structural rise in demand for the
underlying assets, purchase the stock expected to enter the index at relatively low prices weeks
before the entry, and sell it at a higher price to ETFs close to Day 0. This pattern of behavior
appears to be less common among institutional entities, which have longer-term investment
horizons and are less inclined to engage in short-term, low-margin profit-driven activities.

   5.4. Survey of the Global and Israeli Trends in the Crypto Market61

Main Findings

  The  Israeli  public has shown  limited  interest  in  investing  in crypto  assets  thus  far,
   approximating the average extent of investment in developed countries.

  The extent of investment in such assets has risen among Israeli users in view of record Bitcoin
    prices in recent times, relative to the penultimate record level in 2022.

  The data do not attest to meaningful crypto blockchain activity on a commercial scale that may
   be attributed to Israeli users.

   It seems, in part, that Israelis also bought “stablecoins” in order to hedge against changes in
    the NIS-USD exchange rate.

1.     Recent global trends

1.     Recent global trends

volume in this market has been rising in the past half-year in view of the increase in prices of
leading crypto assets, foremost Bitcoin (Figure 1). The estimated market value of these assets has
doubled since early September 2023 and now exceeds USD 2.75 trillion,62 matching the value of





one of the five leading companies in the American stock market (Figure 2). The share of Bitcoin
in the total market of crypto assets stands at around one-half. Bitcoin price, however, is highly

2.      Israel residents’ investments in crypto assets

This box presents, for the first time, quantitative data on the Israeli public’s interest in crypto
assets.63 The data indicate that Israel ranks slightly below average in its share of investment in
these assets among developed countries (Figure 5).

In nominal terms, Israelis’ holdings are estimated at USD 1 billion. The long-term trend
indicates that at times when Bitcoin price was high, the public increased its investment in this asset
above and beyond the effect of price on the value of its holdings. That is to say, when the price of
Bitcoin was high, domestic interest increased as well. Furthermore, at the current peak period,
Israelis have stepped up the extent of their investment relative to the previous peak as compared
with the benchmark countries (Figure 6). In absolute terms, however, their exposure remains small.

Today, several licensed service providers in Israel are active in the field of crypto assets
(virtual assets), offering trading, custodial, and other services. Users are also able to open and
manage personal wallets on the blockchain without using an intermediary.

The Bank of Israel's Financial Stability Report is published twice a year. In the report, the Bank's
 economists provide their assessments regarding the main risks to the financial system, analyze the main
 exposures, and assess potential stress scenarios. The assessments and analyses are based on a review
 of developments during the reviewed period, an examination of the structural changes in the financial
 system, use of analytical models, and an assessment of the background conditions in the global and
 domestic economies. The report presents the risks that could affect the financial system in the short
 and medium terms should they materialize, with the goal of enhancing awareness of them among
 policymakers and the public, and of enabling suitable preparations.

1. INTRODUCTION AND HIGHLIGHTS

1.1 The framework and structure of the report

The Financial Stability Report for the second half of 2021 assesses the stability of the domestic financial system
based on an assessment of the environment in which the system operates—the macroeconomic situation, the
asset markets, credit to households, and credit to the business sector—and an analysis of the resilience of the
financial institutions. The Report thus provides an indication of the economy's various exposures to shocks
originating in Israel and abroad. Based on the review of the developments, the analytical models, the findings
of the Financial Stability Monitor, and an analysis of the financial institutions' resilience, the Report presents
the financial system's risk channels and formulates assessments of the risks to the economy. The Report also

the financial system's risk channels and formulates assessments of the risks to the economy. The Report also
presents risk scenarios as derived from the economy's financial exposures, which pose a threat to continued
economic activity.

1.3 Boxes in the Report

Box 1. Cryptographic assets and financial stability

The global market for crypto asset continued to grow in 2021 and the rate of growth even accelerated. This
included an expanded range of financial services and cryptographic assets, which also includes stablecoins that
can facilitate the rapid and efficient execution of financial transactions. Accompanying the increasing value and
ubiquity of crypto assets is the growing potential for the creation of various threats to financial stability. These
are primarily related to the high volatility of crypto asset prices. However, this market is still small relative to the
global financial market, and the trading platforms for crypto assets are not yet integrated into the traditional

global financial market, and the trading platforms for crypto assets are not yet integrated into the traditional
financial markets in Israel. The direct exposure of financial institutions in Israel to this market is very limited and
according to various surveys the scope of trade in these assets in Israel is not significant relative to other countries.
Box 2. The development of the risks in the activity of nonbank credit providers

Since the beginning of 2020, the number of nonbank credit providers that have raised capital on the Tel Aviv Stock
Exchange has doubled, accompanied by a rapid recovery in the volume of credit provided by these institutions
(following a significant drop in activity at the height of the crisis). The growth in credit during the period being
analyzed was concentrated in the construction and real estate industry. In addition, it appears that the nonbank
entities tried to reduce risks based on the lessons learned from the crisis; however, their activity is still characterized
by risks, such as concentration in a small number of customers and short-term sources of financing. Nonetheless,

by risks, such as concentration in a small number of customers and short-term sources of financing. Nonetheless,
in view of their small share of business credit (less than 2 percent), we do not identify any systemic risk to financial
stability arising from it.
Box 3. The use of consumer loans to finance home purchases

In view of the growth in new mortgages, we examined the use of consumer loans (“loans for any purpose”) in order
to finance a home purchase and the effect of such loans on the leverage ratios for recipients of new mortgages
in Israel. It was found that in the case of at least 15 percent of new mortgages provided between September
2017 and June 2021 (inclusive), the borrower also obtained a supplementary consumer loan from the banks or
a credit card company. Furthermore, it was found that in the case of about one-half of the supplementary loans
they constitute over 5 percent of the value of the home being purchased. This phenomenon may have regulatory
implications by way of its effect on the actual leverage ratio of mortgage recipients, the level of the mortgage's

implications by way of its effect on the actual leverage ratio of mortgage recipients, the level of the mortgage's
risk and also the calculation of the weight of the bank's risk assets and the confinement of its capital in order to
meet capital adequacy requirements.

2.1.1 General

materialize, which was due to, among other things, expansionary monetary and fiscal policy, as well as the effect
of the unexpectedly rapid recovery in advanced economies. The financial conditions in most countries remained
expansionary, although there are growing concerns among investors of a significant slowing in the rate of recovery,
primarily in the developing economies, and also the persistence of global inflation. The COVID-19 pandemic is

without a full lockdown during the period being surveyed. This was to a large extent due to the efficiency of the

2.1.2 The domestic environment

The second half of the year ended in an atmosphere of almost complete return to routine with regard to the risk of
infection and economic risk, and as a result restrictions were lifted, apart from those applying to incoming tourism.
However, the beginning of the second half of the year was overshadowed by the Delta variant and the renewed
restrictions on economic activity, primarily by means of the Green Pass which limited cultural and recreational
activity. The spread of the Omicron variant at the end of 2021 led to renewed restrictions on entering Israel. The
increase in infections has not yet led to a significant decline in economic activity and demand, although the level
of economic activity is still lower than the long-term trend in GDP that would have been expected if the COVID-19

of economic activity is still lower than the long-term trend in GDP that would have been expected if the COVID-19
pandemic had not occurred. During the first half of the year, the employment rate increased rapidly; however,
during the second half the rate of recovery in employment slowed and the broad unemployment rate remained
high. During this period, the Knesset approved the 2021–22 budget and the Arrangements Law, and as a result
uncertainty with regard to fiscal policy declined. The deficits for 2022 and 2023 are expected to be 3.7 percent and
3.4 percent, respectively. According the Research Department's forecast, economic activity will not return to the
level that was expected prior to the crisis until the end of 2023.

2.1.3 The global environment

Financial conditions remained expansionary in many countries, and in particular the advanced economies, a
situation that is supported by the continuing rise in equity indices and the expectation of continued expansionary
policy in coming years. In response to the increase in inflation, many central banks around the world began
to limit their accommodative monetary policies. This was accomplished by, among other things, interest rate
increases, reduced acquisition of government bonds and “forward guidance” regarding their intention to adopt
contractionary measures. Nonetheless, monetary policy remained accommodative and at this stage the change
in policy constitutes a transition to a less accommodative policy rather than a contractionary policy.

prices. The belief that these increases are transitory is still common among experts in the capital market and
senior officials in central banks. Nonetheless, toward the end of the period there was increasing risk that inflation
will be more persistent than what was originally believed. In this context, note that the increase in inflation at this
stage is not being rolled over into an acceleration in wage increases in Europe.6 In contrast, in the US there are

2.2.1 General

Convenient financial conditions characterized most of the global markets during the period being surveyed and

significant gaps relative to the past between financial asset prices and corporate earnings.

2.2.2 Financial assets: bonds and shares

Corporate bonds
The yield spreads between corporate bonds and government bonds are currently at a historic low (after they
rose during the COVID-19 crisis and then returned to their pre-crisis level; see Figure 1). In order to estimate the
extent of separation between the various levels of risk, we examined the variation in spreads between various
ratings:12 AA, BBB and A. An examination of the variation in spreads between the groups (Figure 2) shows that the
gap between each pair of rating groups is at a historic 10-year low. This finding indicates that the spreads are in
part reflecting the separation between the different risk levels of the ratings. An examination of the variation in
spreads according to rating in the US shows a similar situation.

The leading players in the corporate bond market are the mutual funds, which serve as an investment channel for
the public.13 The COVID-19 crisis illustrated the risk of a sharp decline in prices in the markets, and in particular

which are more exposed to rapid withdrawals than medium-to-long term savings channels, i.e., pension funds,
executive insurance plans and provident funds. The mutual funds experienced large net redemptions (which

2.2.3 The real estate market

The housing market

The COVID-19 crisis did not reduce demand for housing, and starting from the end of 2020 there was even an
increase in demand among all groups of buyers. It may be that the Central Bureau of Statistics (CBS) reports of a
sharp drop in the rate of building starts during the second quarter of 2020 contributed to this outcome. First-time
home buyers returned to the market, following the conclusion of the Buyer's Price program. Home upgraders
returned to the market after a long period in which it was difficult to sell an existing home and therefore they had
given up on the idea of purchasing a new one.19 Purchases by investors were incentivized by the lowering of the
purchase tax on investment homes at the end of July 2020.20 On October 30, 2021, the government declared an

purchase tax on investment homes at the end of July 2020.20 On October 30, 2021, the government declared an
increase in the rate of the purchase tax on investors to the level it was set at in June 2015, and on November 28,
2021 the tax hike went into effect. The expectation of a tax hike led to an acceleration in purchases by investors
already prior to November.21 The tax increase is expected to cool off investor demand, based on past experience.
The crisis's effect on supply in the short run was relatively limited, which was a result of the exemption of the
construction industry from the lockdown restrictions, and therefore there was a relatively minor reduction
in building starts (1.3 percent) during 2020 relative to 2019. Central Bureau of Statistics data for the first three

in building starts (1.3 percent) during 2020 relative to 2019. Central Bureau of Statistics data for the first three
quarters of 2021 show an increase of 4.5 percent in housing starts in contrast to the same period in 2020. The
annual rate is 56,100 housing units, which may even be revised upward since the rate of new building permits was
even higher. The crisis led to a lengthening in construction time of about two months on average in 2020 relative
to 2019 and as a result, housing completions in 2020 were lower by 5.8 percent than in 2019, a phenomenon that
continued in 2021 as well.

3. Main stress scenarios for the global economy and the risk to the Israeli economy in the
event of their realization

3. Main stress scenarios for the global economy and the risk to the Israeli economy in the
event of their realization

In this section, we present the main economic risk scenarios for which realization is liable, in our estimation, to
adversely affect the financial system in Israel. The risk scenarios presented in the report were selected on the
basis of the risk of their realization and the adverse impact they are liable to cause to the Israeli economy, based
on its unique characteristics and the fact that it is a small and open economy. The risk scenarios presented here
are based primarily on the surveys and reports of international organizations such as the IMF.

3.1 Inflation risk

With the exit from the COVID-19 crisis, a number of factors developed that tend to support inflation: on the supply
side, the restrictions in order to reduce the spread of infection and the problems in the supply and production
chains; and on the demand side, the shift of private consumption to goods at the expense of services, broad
fiscal support of employment (and assistance to the unemployed), low financing costs and the accumulation of
pent-up demand. As a result of these factors, the CPI—and in some cases the core index as well—rose in many
countries, and their inflation rate is now higher than the central banks' inflation targets. The estimates of analysts
in the capital market and of senior officials in the central banks around the world—although the estimates have

in the capital market and of senior officials in the central banks around the world—although the estimates have
changed somewhat recently—is that most of the inflation is transitory and therefore is expected to taper off in the
near future. If it turns out that inflation persists for longer than expected, it is liable to bring about an acceleration
in the rate of monetary contraction, a decline in the pace of economic recovery, and a deterioration in financial
conditions.
Inflation in Israel has risen, but it is still located within the bounds of the Bank of Israel's target range and so are
the expectations of inflation for various ranges. Nonetheless, global inflation is liable to be “imported” to Israel by

3.2 A sharp decline in asset prices

Some of the widely used risk indicators point to gaps between the pricing of global equity prices and fundamentals,
and against that background there is a risk that equities will be repriced. Among the factors that are liable to bring
this about are changes in the discount rate (as discussed above), underperformance relative to profit/revenue
forecasts, and an increase in the risk premium for equities. A decline in the profitability of companies due to, for
example, a tapering of expansionary fiscal policy, which has supported corporate profitability during the past
two years, is liable to bring about sharp declines in the equity markets, an increase in risk spreads in the business

two years, is liable to bring about sharp declines in the equity markets, an increase in risk spreads in the business
sector, and an increase in the rate of business bankruptcies. In parallel, there will be a negative wealth effect
among investors, which is likely to moderate private consumption and economic activity.

Regulation and policy—the current situation worldwide

Blockchain technology in general, and the crypto market in particular, have the potential to improve the
economic system and increase its efficiency. However, this also involves regulatory challenges, in view of
the anonymity of crypto assets and the lack of uniform global regulation, which are creating significant
information gaps. First, monitoring the service providers in the crypto market is complicated, limited and in
some cases unreliable. The information is produced voluntarily by the companies themselves or provided
by surveys, and there is a lack of uniform regulation. Therefore, the information does not accurately reflect
developments in the market. Furthermore, service providers in the crypto world offer their products on a

developments in the market. Furthermore, service providers in the crypto world offer their products on a
global level and independent of their physical location, a fact that makes regulation and local enforcement
even more difficult. The lack of uniform global regulation creates numerous lacunae which can be exploited
by crypto traders in order to avoid domestic restrictions.
Therefore, international authorities recommend that state regulators adopt global standards and guidelines
also in the crypto assets market, as reflected in the FATF requirements and the IMF recommendations.20,21

It is important to note that these changes in the sources of financing are evidence of diminished risk in

  Types of complementary consumer loans for home purchases

There are a number of situations in which a customer may obtain a complementary consumer loan for the
   purchase of a dwelling together with a mortgage. Let us begin by distinguishing a number of main cases:
   A consumer loan that serves to directly complete the down-payment: Customers that do not have the entire
   down-payment to purchase a dwelling, or who would like to lower the LTV rate of their mortgage, can try
   to complete what is missing by taking out a consumer loan. Such loans can be taken either from the bank
   that provides the mortgage or from another credit provider (another bank, including the bank at which the
   customer's current account is managed, a credit card company, or a nonbank credit provider). This loan is

customer's current account is managed, a credit card company, or a nonbank credit provider). This loan is
   received before the mortgage is signed in order to directly pay the sellers a portion of the required down-
   payment.
   A loan that indirectly completes the down-payment: Such loans are taken out in order to finance expenses
   that are incidental to the purchase of a dwelling, including unexpected expenses, such as payment to the
   lawyer, purchase tax, agency costs, private mortgage consulting, renovations, moving costs, furnishing, an
   increase in the Index of Construction Inputs, and more. While such loans are not used to directly complete
   the down payment, they basically do have an impact on the leverage ratio, since they free up money that

the down payment, they basically do have an impact on the leverage ratio, since they free up money that
   would be used to cover those incidental expenses that would otherwise need to be taken into account in
    calculating the available funds for the purchase of the dwelling. Such loans can also be taken from either
   the bank that provides the mortgage or from a third-party lender. In contrast to loans that are used to
    directly pay the down-payment, which are received before the mortgage is signed, these loans can also be
   taken out afterwards.
   Synergy loans: These loans carry improved terms (lower interest rates and spread out over longer periods)
   that are sometimes offered to customers who move their banking activity to the bank that issues them

that are sometimes offered to customers who move their banking activity to the bank that issues them
   the mortgage. Synergy loans can be attractive to customers, since they are provided under good terms,
   sometimes even better than those of the mortgage, and can therefore be taken out even in cases when
   there is enough for a down payment. Synergy loans also make it possible to lower the leverage rate,
   thereby improving the terms of the mortgage. For example, lowering the leverage rate to below 60 percent
  may greatly improve the terms of the mortgage. It is worth noting that on October 6, 2021, the Banking

The scope and nature of complementary loans

We examine the scope of use of complementary loans in the Israeli mortgage market. In order to identify
the complementary loans, we use the Bank of Israel's Credit Data Register. The Register documents all
credit transactions of customers in Israel, thereby enabling us to identify consumer loans that were
received around the time a new mortgage was taken out. There is some difficulty in identifying and
classifying complementary loans for the purchase of a dwelling, since the Register does not contain specific
classifications of such loans. The loans are therefore identified as consumer loans that are received around
the time of the new mortgage. We have defined such loans as all-purpose consumer loans issued to a

the time of the new mortgage. We have defined such loans as all-purpose consumer loans issued to a
customer in the month in which he took out a mortgage, or within a month after taking out a mortgage.2
The main assumption in identifying the complementary loans is that a consumer loan taken out around the
time of a new mortgage was either used as part of the payment for the dwelling or had an impact on the LTV
rate for the dwelling by freeing up money from incidental payments.
After identifying all of the complementary loans, we classified them as loans that were apparently used to
complete down-payments or loans that were apparently issued as synergy loans. Loans were classified as
synergy loans if they fulfilled four conditions: the loan was issued by the bank from which the mortgage was

synergy loans if they fulfilled four conditions: the loan was issued by the bank from which the mortgage was
taken; the loan was large (more than NIS 75,000); it was taken out for a long period (more than 5 years); and
it carried improved terms (an interest rate that is lower than prime-1 percent). The rest of the loans were
classified as loans to complete the down-payment, and were divided among lenders (the bank from which
the mortgage was received, a different bank, or a credit card company).
It should be emphasized that the analysis deals only with complementary loans from banks and credit card
companies (which are obligated to report to the Central Credit Register), and does not include loans from

companies (which are obligated to report to the Central Credit Register), and does not include loans from

   Regulatory and prudential implications

A loan to complete the down payment may increase the customer's risk in a number of ways. First, loans
   to finance down payments are generally more expensive and for a shorter term than mortgages, which
   makes them less appropriate for financing the purchase of a dwelling. Second, complementary loans are
   generally taken out before the mortgage, and their future repayments have an effect on the calculation of
   the customer's disposable income, which may have a negative impact on the terms of the mortgage itself.
    In contrast with loans, which the customer takes out in order to complete the down payment, synergy loans
   are generally presented as a benefit for moving activity to the bank, and are not necessarily connected

are generally presented as a benefit for moving activity to the bank, and are not necessarily connected
   to mortgage borrowing. However, such loans also may have prudential and regulatory implications. First,
   synergy loans, even if they are issued for longer terms relative to regular consumer loans, are generally for
   shorter terms than mortgages, which increases total payments during the initial period. Second, synergy
   loans will impact the mix of the mortgage by increasing the part of the mortgage that is indexed to the
   prime rate. (Consumer loans in general, and complementary loans in particular, are generally indexed to
   the prime rate.) Finally, taking out a large synergy loan together with a mortgage may have an impact on

the prime rate.) Finally, taking out a large synergy loan together with a mortgage may have an impact on
   the customer's LTV rate, and thereby on the calculation of the bank's risk weighted assets. For instance,
    let's say that a customer needs NIS 700,000 to finance the purchase of a property that is worth NIS 1 million.
   The customer has NIS 300,000 of equity, and can therefore take out a loan with an LTV rate of 70 percent.
   However, one of the mortgage banks offers him a large loan of NIS 110,000 with excellent terms on condition

the customer can choose to take a mortgage of NIS 590,000 together with the synergy loan, thereby lowering

bank's risk-weighted assets and on its capital confinement for the purpose of meeting the capital adequacy
requirements, even though the customer's total LTV for purchasing the dwelling is 70 percent.

MAIN FINDINGS

•   The risk of a global recession increased during the period being surveyed, against the background of increased
    geopolitical risks and the acceleration of inflation, and in turn the tightening of monetary policy worldwide.
   These factors have also led to price declines in the financial markets.
•  On the macro level, Israel stands out positively among the OECD countries. Although inflation is higher than
    the target, it is lower than in other advanced economies; the labor market is tight; and economic growth is
    relatively strong.
•   Credit to businesses and households expanded rapidly in 2022, following a similar expansion in the preceding
    year. Nonetheless, signs began appearing in April 2022 of a moderation in the rate of growth in credit, in view

year. Nonetheless, signs began appearing in April 2022 of a moderation in the rate of growth in credit, in view
    of the increase in the interest rate and in yields in the economy.
•   Equity prices in Israel declined during the second half of 2022, as they did in numerous other countries, while
    corporate bond spreads in Israel rose moderately. Despite the decline in stock prices, the long-term PE ratio
     is not low in historical terms.
•  Home prices increased during the period being surveyed, a continuation of the upward trend that reappeared
    in the second half of 2021, and the ratio of home prices to fundamentals reached a record in historical terms.
THE STRUCTURE OF THE REPORT AND ITS GOAL1

The Financial Stability Report for the Second Half of 2022 examines the changes that occurred in the financial
system during this period according to three main exposure channels: the macroeconomic environment, the asset
markets, and credit to households and the business sector. As such, it provides an indicator of the economy’s
various exposures to shocks originating in Israel and the rest of the world. Based on the survey of developments,
the analytical models, and the Financial Stability Monitor, we describe the financial system’s channels of exposure
and use them to formulate our assessment of the risks to the economy. The report also presents a risk scenario
that is based on the financial system’s exposures to global markets, a scenario that, should it materialize, is liable

that is based on the financial system’s exposures to global markets, a scenario that, should it materialize, is liable
to threaten the continuity of economic activity. The appendix to this report provides additional details about the
structure of the report and the logic behind it.

1. The challenges to the economy and the main channels of exposure

Economic policy makers are currently dealing with the challenge of restraining inflation, which requires monetary
tightening. This is in view of the high level of prices in the housing market; a period of increasing leverage among
households and companies operating in the housing market; and an increase in global geopolitical risk.

   3. What explains the changes in the fair value of commercial real estate?

The above analysis of commercial real estate performance shows that the main phenomenon to be
   explained is the change in fair value: There was a gradual decline in the income return, which is reflected in
   the increase in real estate asset values, while in contrast, there are years with exceptionally large fluctuations
    in real estate asset values. It is well known that changes in real estate prices primarily reflect changes
   and expected changes in supply and demand. The home price index, for example, is based on actual
   transactions which reflect changes and expectations. In contrast, there is no systematic methodological
   index for commercial real estate and the value of commercial real estate assets is usually measured using

index for commercial real estate and the value of commercial real estate assets is usually measured using
   valuations based on the DCF method. Therefore, the changes in fair value should primarily reflect changes
    in the assets’ fundamentals.
    In the DCF system, the expected flow of revenue from rentals is discounted. In principle, the expected flow
    of revenue is the asset’s area multiplied by the expected occupancy rate and by the expected rental income
   per square meter according to the contracts that have been signed (for further discussion, see below). The
   discounting of the cash flow is carried out by means of a capitalization rate, which is determined during the

discounting of the cash flow is carried out by means of a capitalization rate, which is determined during the
   valuation and is sometimes supported by actual transactions in similar assets. As a result, this method is
   based primarily on a number of parameters (fundamentals): the space of the asset, the rate of occupancy,
   the rent from the asset and the capitalization rate. The average rent from an asset is in general determined
   by the characteristics of the asset and those of the contract,10 while the capitalization rate reflects the
    asset’s risk premium and the risk-free interest rate, as in the case of financial assets.

   6. Conclusion

The commercial real estate industry accounts for a considerable share of the financial system and it is
   important to analyze its performance and the valuation of commercial real estate assets relative to
   fundamentals. The analysis presented here shows that starting in 2010, there has been a gradual decline
    in the return on rentals, though it wasn’t uniform across the different asset types. An econometric analysis
   found that actual monthly rental income—one of the most important fundamentals in asset valuation—
   explains only part of the change in fair value. Furthermore, there appears to be an upward trend in the ratio
    of asset value per unit of area (in square meters) to monthly rental income per square meter, which may

    indicate expectations of growth and an increase in the value of commercial real estate that is not reflected in

2. THE TIMELINE AND THE EFFECT OF EVENTS ON THE COMPANIES INVOLVED

A series of events between May and August 2022 exposed serious problems in the behavior of Unet Credit
Finance Services and Gibui Holdings. These events led to the collapse of their shares, concerns over their
ability to pay their debts, and investigations by regulatory bodies and the police. The associated events
were monitored by searching through the reports to the public by Unet and Gibui in the Tel Aviv Stock
Exchange’s “Maya” system, and through searches of relevant press articles using the Google search engine.
The decision on what the most significant events were is, obviously, a judgment call, but we based it
not only on experience and expertise, but also on the reaction of the companies’ shares to the events in
question (Figure 1).20

The average daily return on Unet Credit shares on the days when the first significant negative events that
we identified transpired was -17 percent. A number of days after that, trading in the company’s shares was
halted, and when trading resumed, the share immediately dropped by an additional 55 percent and did
not resume trading. Gibui Holdings shares actually continued trading throughout most of the period. In the
last seven negative events that we identified between July and August 2022, the company’s shares fell by
more than 20 percent on average in response to each event. It therefore seems that investors interpreted
the events at Unet and Gibui as destructive to the value of those companies.

3. METHODOLOGY AND DATA

3.1 Data

For each company in the nonbank credit provision industry, the daily return (adjusted for dividends) on
their shares was calculated for each day during the period around the events described above. Statistical
examinations based on a test of the impact of each event on the shares of each of the companies in the
industry separately may be problematic if there is a correlation between the companies’ shares on each of
the examined days. In order to deal with this concern, we examined the impact of the events not only on the
shares of the individual companies, but also on the weighted portfolio of the industry. For this purpose, we
built two synthetic portfolios of the companies in the nonbank credit provision industry, excluding Gibui

The shares of the nonbank credit companies traded on the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange are affected not only by
investors’ assessments of the nonbank credit companies, but also by macroeconomic and financial events

3.2 Methodology

3.2 Methodology

In order to examine the effect of the events at Gibui Holdings and Unet Credit on the other companies in the
nonbank credit market, as assessed by the financial markets in real time, we use an event study method. It
is worth noting that these events were unexpected and that each of them had a significant impact on the
probability that Gibui Holdings or Unet Credit would collapse. The focus of our interest in this box is not
the examination of the negative impact on the involved companies themselves, but rather on the question
of whether and to what extent the negative events at the two companies reflect broader problems in the
nonbank credit market.21

A negative response by shares of competing companies to a worsening in the state of Gibui Holdings or Unet
Credit may be due to investors’ assessments that the problems in the two companies are an indication of
broader problems in the nonbank credit market and/or an assessment that the two companies’ problems
would lead to more severe regulation or a worsening of market conditions for the other companies in the
industry. In contrast, a positive reaction by competitors’ shares may be due to investors’ assessments
that the level of competition in the nonbank credit market would decline due to the collapse of two of
the competitors, and that this would lead to an increase in the profitability of the other companies in the
market.

In order to examine the effect of the collapse of Gibui Holdings and Unet Credit on investors’ assessments
regarding the state of the competing nonbank credit companies, we examined the response of the portfolios
of the shares of the competing companies to the events, while controlling for the appropriate benchmark
indices. For this purpose, we adopted the method used, for example, by Wan and Wong (2009). Specifically,
we estimated the following equation:

The nonbank credit market has grown rapidly in recent years, but in view of the slight prudential regulation,
   there have also been concerns of the stability of companies in this field. These concerns escalated with the
    revelation of evidence of significant mismanagement at the Unet Credit and Gibui Holdings companies
    in the spring and summer of 2022. Specifically they raise questions regarding whether these problematic
   events are the domain of two particular companies, or whether they indicate a broader problem in the
   nonbank credit industry. The failures discovered at Unet Credit and at Gibui Holdings may indicate similar
    failures in other companies in the industry, which may lead to problems in those companies as well and/

failures in other companies in the industry, which may lead to problems in those companies as well and/
   or to stricter regulation on them, which would come with costs to shareholders. This point of view was
   expressed not only in the public discourse, but also in the new and stringent guidelines issued by the
    Israel Securities Authority. In contrast, if the events that took place at the two companies are perceived as
    isolated incidents in those companies only, which have no broad impact on the industry as a whole, then
   the collapse of these two companies may help their competitors.

We examined the shares of Unet Credit and Gibui Holdings, and found that investors did in fact interpret
   the events at those companies as very negative in terms of their valuations. In view of the two conflicting
   hypotheses regarding the impact on the competing companies, this study examines the equity market’s
   assessment of the impact of these events on the other companies in the nonbank credit industry, on the
   basis of the understanding that the financial markets can serve as a leading indicator of the future effects
    of present events. In particular, we used the event study method, focusing on the effect of the various
   negative events that took place at Unet Credit and Gibui Holdings on the competing companies.

The findings show that the negative events at Unet Credit and Gibui Holdings did not have a statistically or
economically significant effect on the shares of the competing nonbank credit companies. The events at
Unet Credit and Gibui Holdings may have been perceived by investors—perhaps contrary to the sentiment
in the media—as isolated, and not as broad events with implications for all companies in the industry.
However, the large companies in the industry had a moderate positive reaction, compared with the
moderate negative reaction of the small companies in the industry. This provides a hint that investors did
perceive the events at the two collapsing companies as having some broad impact; they were expected to

perceive the events at the two collapsing companies as having some broad impact; they were expected to
have a negative effect on the other small companies in the industry, but to help the larger companies due
to an expected decline in the level of competition in the industry due to the collapse of the two companies
and an increase in the regulatory threshold for activity in the industry. Either way, the empirical findings
in this box do not support the hypothesis that the collapse of the two companies was perceived as an
indication of a broad failure that endangers the entire nonbank credit industry. At the very most, it may
have some implications for the level of competition in the industry.
